claims.text: The superconducting transition temperature in equiatomic Ti-Zr-Hf-Nb-Mo high-entropy alloys is governed by electron count.
Equiatomic substitution of Mo by Cr reduces the alloy's overall valence electron concentration.
Substitution of Mo by Cr alters electron-phonon coupling strength.
Substitution of Mo by Cr will produce a measurable shift in Tc.
The starting alloy is equiatomic Ti-Zr-Hf-Nb-Mo.
The starting alloy is a homogeneous solid solution produced by arc melting and homogenization.
The modified alloy is equiatomic Ti-Zr-Hf-Nb-Cr, with every element present above 5 atomic percent.
Both alloys will be arc melted and homogenized under identical conditions, exemplified by 1200 °C for 24 hours.
Altered valence electron concentration changes the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Changes in the density of states at the Fermi level modulate electron-phonon coupling strength.
Changes in electron-phonon coupling alter the superconducting pairing interaction and thereby shift Tc.
Moving VEC toward an optimum may raise Tc, whereas moving it away from the optimum may lower Tc.
The proposed relationship applies only while the alloys remain homogeneous solid solutions satisfying the five-element, at-least-5-at.% constraint.
The proposed relationship is limited to a compositional range in which the electronic structure remains dominated by constituent-element contributions.
The optimal VEC for maximum electron-phonon coupling in these alloys is not precisely established.
Tc can be compared using resistivity and magnetic-susceptibility measurements.
No statistically significant difference in Tc between the alloys would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to attribute a Tc change to a measured VEC-related electronic-structure shift would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention is asserted to reduce VEC, but the specified equiatomic Mo-to-Cr substitution does not change nominal VEC under the usual group-number convention because both Cr and Mo contribute six valence electrons. Thus the proposed intervention does not implement its stated mediator.
